title: Knowing how to die
hook: Guru Nanak: death wouldn't be called bad if people knew how truly to die

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikh bedtime hymns sung at a funeral, and death spoken of as going home. Your line was tucking someone in. Did you hum something as the light went down? Today, a hymn that turns the whole question around. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

A family is mourning. Someone says what people say: what a terrible thing, death. And a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, answers back, gently. On page 579, in a set of verses Guru Nanak gave for times of mourning, comes a line that, put plainly, runs like this: people, don't call death bad, if only someone knew how truly to die. So the hymn doesn't argue that death is pleasant. It moves the problem. The trouble, it suggests, isn't dying. It's not knowing how. Today: what it might mean to know how.
screen: `A FAMILY MOURNS.` → `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` → `IF ONE KNEW HOW.`

segments.voice: Start with the strange part. Death sounds like something that simply happens to you. Nobody takes a class in it. But the hymn speaks of it as a skill, something a person can know or not know. Second, where Sikhs say that skill is learned. In Sikh teaching, as the Gurus describe it, a person who lives remembering the divine Name, serving others and living honestly is already practicing for the end. The same verses speak of serving the Lord and of the true court a person goes to after this life. So knowing how to die isn't a last-minute trick. It's what a whole life has been rehearsing. Third, a phrase Sikhs use for this: dying while alive. Some Sikh readers hear it as letting the ego die now, the grasping, the need to win, so that when death comes there's less left to tear away. Readers explain it in different ways, but the shape is simple. Practice letting go in small things, and the big letting go is less of a stranger. Fourth, an ordinary afternoon. The hymn was given for mourning, but if a whole life is the rehearsal, then the rehearsal is happening this afternoon, in an hour spent scrolling or an hour spent with someone we love. Read that way, the question shifts from how long a life runs to how the hour in front of you is lived. So verses given for mourning spend their breath on how to live.
screen: `DEATH AS A SKILL.` · `LEARNED BY LIVING.` · `DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `THE HOUR YOU'RE IN.` · then, large: `KNOWING HOW.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, look at the next hour of your day. Not the whole week. Just the next hour. Where will you be, and who will be there? Ask one quiet question of it: if this hour were lived well, what would it look like? Maybe slower. Maybe kinder to someone. Maybe one thing done properly instead of three done badly. Let one small picture come, and keep it. If you pray, you can hold that hour up in prayer in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Maran, the Gurmukhi word for death in Guru Nanak's hymn, which says the trouble isn't dying, but not knowing how, learned by living. Today's word.
Your line: knowing how. Today, live one hour well, on purpose, the hour you pictured in the sit. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Gurus' hymns on death in the gurdwara and at funerals, where the evening hymns of Kirtan Sohila are sung; Sikh teaching describes remembering the Name, honest work and service as the way a life prepares for its end.
